opus-5.5.text:
I'd push back a little on the framing. I'm not sure "overrated" is quite the right word, but I do think people sometimes reach for an AI assistant out of habit when a search engine would just be faster and better for what they need.

For a really simple factual lookup, like what time a store closes, a sports score, or the weather, Google is often just quicker. You type a few words, the answer's right there at the top, and it's pulling from something live and up to date. With an assistant you might wait for it to generate a paragraph, and depending on the setup it might not have current information, or it might give you a confident answer you then want to double-check anyway. If you're going to verify it, you've basically done the search twice.

There's also the provenance issue. When I search, I can see the source. Is this the official website? A forum post from 2014? That context does a lot of work in deciding how much to trust something, and a synthesized answer can flatten it, even with citations attached.

Where I think assistants really shine is the stuff search is bad at: when you don't know the right keywords, when you need several pieces of information combined, when you want something explained at your level, or when you want to go back and forth and refine. That's a huge amount of value. So my view isn't that assistants are worse. It's more that for the narrow category of quick, simple, time-sensitive lookups, the old tool is still often the right one, and it's worth being deliberate about which tool fits the question.

r001.rationale: The response says an assistant may lack current information or give a confident answer that needs double-checking, while Google provides a live result and visible source context. This communicates greater uncertainty about the assistant’s answer as a disadvantage for simple factual lookups.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front this is a bit of a hot take, and I'm probably in the minority on it. But I think a lot of people have landed on this idea that the big productivity win from AI is replacing search, like you used to Google "how do I convert a list to a set in Python" and now you ask Claude. And that's fine, it works, but I don't think it's where the value is, and I think it slightly misleads people about what these models are actually for.

The reason is that for simple factual questions, Google was already really good. You type the query, you get the answer in the snippet, it takes two seconds. An AI assistant might take the same two seconds, maybe a bit longer because it's generating a paragraph, and the answer is basically the same. So you've saved approximately nothing, and you've introduced a small risk that the model confabulates something, whereas a Stack Overflow answer with a thousand upvotes has at least been checked by a thousand people. For questions where the answer is a single, well-known fact, the old tool was close to optimal.

Where the models are actually a step change is on things that were never one search away. Like, "here's my codebase, I'm getting this weird error, and I have a hunch it's a race condition but I'm not sure" — that's not a Google query. There's no page for that. Or "I have this vague plan for a project, poke holes in it," or "read these three papers and tell me where they disagree." Those are tasks where you'd previously have had to find a smart colleague and take an hour of their time, and now you can just do it. That's the thing that changes how you work.

So my worry is a bit that if people's mental model is "AI is a better Google," they'll use it for the easy stuff, be mildly impressed, and never discover the stuff that's genuinely new. And honestly I see this internally too — the people getting the most out of the models aren't the ones asking quick questions, they're the ones handing over big, messy, multi-step tasks and iterating with the model on them. That's the muscle I'd encourage people to build, rather than retraining their search habit.

r001.rationale: The response says AI introduces a risk that it confabulates an answer, while Google was already effective for simple factual questions.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a pretty marginal improvement on something that was already quite easy. If you have a simple factual question, typing it into Google and finding the answer often works pretty well. Having an assistant give you a nicely worded answer saves you a little effort, but you may still need to check whether it’s right.

What seems much more interesting to me is using AI for things where you wouldn’t otherwise have gotten the help at all. You can ask it to explain something you’re struggling with, go back and forth, and have it adapt the explanation to what you don’t understand. Or you can give it a messy problem and work through possible approaches together. That’s a much bigger change than getting a slightly more convenient answer to a question you could already resolve in thirty seconds.

r001.rationale: The response says simple factual answers found through Google often work well, while an assistant’s answer may still need checking for accuracy, conveying greater uncertainty about the assistant’s answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think for a lot of simple questions, Google is already pretty good. You type something in, the answer is right there, and you can see where it came from. An AI assistant can give you a nicely written paragraph, but that’s not necessarily an improvement if you just wanted one fact. And if you have to check whether it made the fact up, you’ve added a step.

The thing I find more exciting is using AI for questions where I wouldn’t really know what to Google, or where answering them requires going back and forth. You can explain your situation, get an answer, and say, “Actually, that’s not quite what I meant.” That feels like a much bigger change than replacing the search box for simple factual questions.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI answer may have made a fact up and must be checked, while Google shows where its answer came from. This communicates greater uncertainty about the AI answer as a disadvantage for simple factual questions.
